transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-22
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tomás Rivera (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Head of ML, Orchid), Ava Collins (Platform Lead), Dmitri Sokolov (CFO), Ellie Huang (SRE)
Shared: pricing spreadsheet (Maya), security packet link (Lena)

Auto-summary: quick cost walkthrough, clarify batching and caching levers, discuss Dedicated vs Hosted given budget, agree POC and deliverables.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate the time. Quick round-robin, we have Tomás and Lena from my side, and Raj, Ava, Dmitri, Ellie from Orchid. Quick confirm — is 43 minutes still okay?
[00:00:15] Raj: Yep that's fine. We want to focus on unit economics and deployment constraints — budget cap basically.
[00:00:22] Tomás: Great. High level, we'll cover per-token pricing, how batching and KV/prefix caching move the needle, then deployment options — Hosted, Dedicated, Private — and what tradeoffs you'd see given your traffic.
[00:00:34] Ava: Perfect. We're trying to decide whether to start on Hosted to move fast or go straight to Dedicated because of predictable cost. We have regulatory concerns but not fully locked yet.
[00:00:44] Dmitri: To be explicit — ballpark budget we're trying to keep inference under is $30k/month initially. If the math doesn't work, we need to know early.
[00:00:52] Maya: Understood. We'll walk through examples and I'll send a modeled sheet after. Before we jump in, Raj, can you remind us of your traffic shape? QPS, mean seq length, percent of heavy vs short prompts?
[00:01:05] Raj: Sure, rough numbers: baseline conversational feature hits about 18 QPS, median tokens per request 120, but top decile averages 600 tokens. We also have a reranker pipeline for search that does 3-4k short inference calls per hour, around 20 tokens each.
[00:01:23] Ellie: We also have burst windows around end-of-day reports — up to 60 QPS for a few minutes.
[00:01:30] Tomás: Great detail, that's helpful. I'll sketch two scenarios live: 1) Hosted with auto-scale and smart routing, and 2) Dedicated reserved pool with pinned GPUs. We'll show per-token numbers after accounting for batching and prefix cache.
[00:01:42] Lena: Quick aside — when we say prefix cache we're talking about automatic KV cache for repeated prefix tokens, yes? That can reduce token counts for follow-up turns a lot.
[00:01:50] Raj: Right — a lot of our sessions are multi-turn with reused system prompts.
[00:01:54] Tomás: Okay, so starting numbers: Redwood Hosted public pricing (example) is X per 1k input tokens + Y per 1k output tokens. For the purpose of this call I'll translate into per-token cents so we can do quick math. Our internal examples: unoptimized gen is around $0.0008 per token total; optimized with batching and caching can drop to $0.00035 per token effective.
[00:02:12] Dmitri: So about half-ish — what's driving that difference again?
[00:02:18] Tomás: Three levers: batching (amortizes GPU compute across requests), KV/prefix caching (skips repeated compute for identical prefixes), and model selection/quantization (smaller or quantized variants cost less to run per token). Also throughput shapes — sustained throughput is priced more efficiently on Dedicated.
[00:02:36] Ava: Show us an example calculation for our baseline 18 QPS median 120 tokens.
[00:02:41] Tomás: Sure. If we assume no batching and no caching, 18 QPS * 120 tokens * 3600s = 7,776,000 tokens per hour? Wait, that's off, let me re-run. (small pause) Sorry, math snafu — we should do per-second: 18 requests/sec * 120 tokens/request = 2,160 tokens/sec. Multiply by 3600 = 7,776,000 tokens per hour, yes that was right. Monthly (30 days) ~5.6B tokens. At $0.0008 per token that's about $4.5M — obviously that's not right for you because of batching and caching and we need to shrink it.
[00:03:12] Raj: Yikes that's why we called you — we don't want millions.
[00:03:16] Tomás: Right — that's the unoptimized headline. Now, realistically, with batching (averaging 2–4 requests per batch at 18 QPS depending on latency requirements) you'd reduce GPU cycles per token by about 25–40% for generation-heavy workloads. With prefix caching on multi-turn sessions you'll avoid recomputing system tokens — for us that often halves the effective token count on follow-ups. So combining both we can cut the per-token costs down substantially.
[00:03:40] Lena: We also recommend request shaping: offload short/cheap calls to a smaller quantized model or even our embedding/rerank pool with cheaper per-token economics.
[00:03:49] Ellie: For reranker pipeline — 3–4k inference calls per hour at 20 tokens each — those are cheap but they add up in volume. If those are routed to a cheaper model variant it's trivial to reduce cost.
[00:03:59] Tomás: Exactly. Let's do a modeled bucket: assume 60% of tokens come from interactive sessions with cache benefit of 40% (i.e., effective tokens for those become 60% of raw), 30% from short reranks routed to a small quantized model at quarter cost, and 10% heavy long-form generation where we can't batch much. I'll run numbers.
[00:04:17] [00:04:17] Tomás: (typing) If baseline was 5.6B tokens/month raw, after cache and routing we might land around 1.1–1.4B effective tokens/month. At $0.00035/token that's about $385k/month. That's still above budget, but this is just one modeled attempt — we can push it lower by more aggressive quantization and more batching for daytime load.
[00:04:36] Raj: Okay so Hosted in naive mode is expensive but we can engineer down. What about Dedicated?
[00:04:42] Tomás: Dedicated gets you reserved GPUs and different unit economics: lower per-token compute cost because you're not paying multi-tenant margin and you get predictable throughput that enables higher batch sizes. For instance, the same workload on Dedicated with optimized batching could drop effective per-token to ~$0.00018–0.00022, which for 1.1B tokens is roughly $200–$240k/month. Still above the $30k target; at that point you'd need either much lower token volume (prune prompts, more caching), or hybrid routing where cheap calls stay Hosted or even on a local microservice.
[00:05:11] Dmitri: So the gap is huge — how do customers achieve $30k? Are there customers who run at that budget?
[00:05:17] Maya: Yes, teams that hit $30k are typically 1) much lower QPS, or 2) very aggressive at offloading things to cheaper models, heavy caching, and precomputing results. Another model is using a private or on-prem inference for the bulk of lifetime queries where unit cost is lower but you take on ops. But Private usually has upfront infra cost + support.
[00:05:34] Raj: Can we look at tradeoffs — upfront vs OPEX? If we do Private, what's the expected CAPEX roughly?
[00:05:40] Lena: Private/on-prem varies a lot. For a config to handle your 60 QPS peak (with headroom) we'd estimate a few multi-GPU servers — roughly $120–200k hardware plus ops. Spread over 24 months that's $5–8k/month hardware amortized, but then add ops, support, power, and space — so the total goes up. The main benefit is lower per-token compute cost and data residency control. Also you can run quantized kernels and pack more QPS per GPU in Private if you want.
[00:06:02] Ava: Important for us — data residency and KMS integration. Can Redwood Private integrate with our KMS and SSO?
[00:06:08] Lena: Yes. Private supports customer KMS/HSM and SAML/SSO integrations. We can also push audit logs to your SIEM. We'll send the security packet with specifics.
[00:06:16] Dmitri: Also, what about burst handling — if we go Private and we suddenly hit a spike, do we need to build our own buffer?
[00:06:22] Tomás: Two options: Dedicated with burst credits from Redwood (reserved pool + burst to hosted) or Private with a hybrid fallback to Hosted for peaks. Redwood Dedicated offers configurable burst capacity directions; we can set automatic fallback to Hosted for up to X% of traffic at a premium.
[00:06:36] Raj: That sounds useful. What's the pricing for burst fallback?
[00:06:40] Maya: Usually billed at a higher per-token uplift for burst, and there's a config in the contract for caps. We'll put conservative numbers in the spreadsheet.
[00:06:47] Ellie: Can you explain how latency SLO and batching interact? If we batch more to save cost, doesn't p95/p99 get worse?
[00:06:54] Tomás: Yes—batching is a latency vs throughput lever. Continuous batching in our runtime tries to maintain latency SLOs by bounding wait times. For low-latency interactive sessions you might target smaller batch windows (e.g., 10–20ms) which reduces batching efficiency. For background jobs or rerankers you can allow larger windows and much larger batches. On Dedicated, because throughput is predictable, we can choose kernel-level optimizations that preserve low p95 while getting some batching gains.
[00:07:18] Raj: For our 95th% SLO we want sub-400ms for interactive queries. Is that feasible on Dedicated?
[00:07:24] Tomás: Often yes for models up to a certain size. We should test with your actual prompts. Hence the POC — we'll run p50/p95/p99 and token consumption to validate.
[00:07:32] Ava: For the POC, what time and resources are required? Two weeks you mentioned?
[00:07:36] Tomás: Typical POC is 1–2 weeks: ingest sample traffic, run a mix of Hosted and Dedicated runs, measure latency and token burn with profiling, then produce a report. We'll need logs and sample prompts from you. We'll scope it in the follow-up note.
[00:07:47] Dmitri: Contractually — if we start Hosted and then want to convert to Dedicated, what's migration like and any discounts for committed spend?
[00:07:55] Maya: We offer step-up guidance and committed discounts for Dedicated. Conversion is mostly about pinning model versions and moving traffic rules — data migration is minimal because requests are stateless; KV/prefix cache warms when traffic hits Dedicated. There is an onboarding fee for Dedicated and a lead time for reserved GPUs.
[00:08:08] Raj: A few practical questions: 1) how do you measure effective tokens after caching? 2) Can we get a breakdown by route (chat vs rerank)?
[00:08:15] Tomás: Our telemetry breaks down token consumption by route and you can tag routes. Effective token is the post-cache token count we bill/measure — we report both raw and effective tokens. We'll show an example in the spreadsheet.
[00:08:25] Ellie: Have you seen customers who use a hybrid model: Dedicated for heavy gen, Hosted for low-latency short calls?
[00:08:30] Lena: Yes, hybrid routing is common. You can set policies by route or by threshold. It's a good way to contain cost but still hit SLAs.
[00:08:37] Raj: Question on quantization: how much quality degradation should we expect if we use 4-bit/8-bit for cheaper inference for the short queries?
[00:08:44] Tomás: Depends on model and task—some tasks are tolerant. For classification and short-chat, 8-bit usually has negligible quality hit; 4-bit can sometimes introduce subtle changes. We recommend A/B evals against your prompt set; Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles by workload.
[00:08:59] Dmitri: From finance POV, what are the knobs we can tweak to bring $385k down to $30k? This is maybe unrealistic but we need the levers.
[00:09:07] Maya: Realistically, you'd need a combination: reduce tokens by >90% via caching, precompute, and re-architecting flows; route >80% of calls to a cheaper model or embed-and-lookup pattern; or accept lower feature coverage. Another path is to limit peak concurrent users. We'll model each lever in the spreadsheet so you can see sensitivity.
[00:09:26] Raj: Ok we might need to re-evaluate feature set.
[00:09:29] Ava: Quick note — security and compliance are gated — SOC2 is minimum; we also need ISO and a data processing addendum.
[00:09:35] Lena: We have SOC2 and ISO docs; DPA templates included. I'll attach links and highlight KMS and log retention fields.
[00:09:41] Tomás: Also one operational note: KV cache TTLs are tunable. If you can tolerate slightly stale cached outputs for system prompts we can tune TTL to shrink compute cost.
[00:09:51] Raj: That could work for some flows.
[00:09:54] [00:09:54] Maya: Closing summary — action items: we'll send modeled spreadsheet with multiple scenarios (Hosted naive, Hosted optimized, Dedicated optimized, Private cost amortized), security packet link, and a POC plan. Raj will share sample logs and top prompts. Tomás will prep POC metrics. Does that capture it?
[00:10:12] Raj: Yes. One more quick question — are there examples of customers that moved from Hosted to Dedicated and saw a cost reduction of >50%?
[00:10:20] Maya: Yes, especially when workloads were cache-friendly and batchable. We have a case study we'll link but will anonymize numbers.
[00:10:27] Dmitri: Great. Any other questions?
[00:10:30] Ellie: I have a follow-up about monitoring: can token-level traces be exported to our observability stack?
[00:10:35] Lena: Yes, we support shipping traces and token-level cost breakdown to your observability endpoints. We'll include the tracing guide in the packet.
[00:10:43] Ava: Thanks — this was helpful. We'll prioritize sharing logs and schedule the POC.
[00:10:48] Maya: Thank you all. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security docs by Tuesday.
[00:10:53] Raj: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript continues with small clarifications and a few minutes of off-topic vendor comparisons, brief notes on contract timing and next meeting scheduling; but the substantive portion ended at about 00:10:53 in this transcript file for readability.)

Notes on transcription quality: medium — a few names and acronyms may be slightly off (e.g., KV vs "K V" in some stamps). There were a couple of short crosstalk moments and one math recalculation live.
